title: Shvetaketu comes home
word: reading the Isha in the original
hook: a boy comes home after twelve years of study, proud and missing one thing
carry: vidya: learning that frees, not learning that puffs up
tomorrow: can a king with a crown teach a monk about freedom?

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirguna and saguna, beyond form and with a face, from Gargi's two questions. Today the Isha says something that sounds like a warning against learning itself.
screen: `NIRGUNA AND SAGUNA.` · `NOW: A WARNING ABOUT LEARNING?`

segments.voice: A boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, and the Chandogya Upanishad, telling his story, doesn't flatter him: conceited, thinking himself learned, stiff with it. His father, Uddalaka, lets him settle in. Then he asks one question. Did you ask your teachers for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Twelve years of study, and Shvetaketu has to say: no. What is that teaching?
screen: `AWAY AT TWELVE. HOME AT TWENTY-FOUR.` → `PROUD.` → `DID YOU ASK FOR THE ONE TEACHING?` → `NO.`

segments.voice: Hold that boy in mind and read Isha nine. Andham tamah pravishanti ye avidyam upasate: into blind darkness go those who worship not-knowing. Fair. Then: into greater darkness, as it were, go those who delight in knowing alone. That's Shvetaketu at twenty-four. Two small words keep it from being an attack on learning. Iva, as it were: a picture, not a verdict. And ratah, delighting in, as if learning were the whole point. Verse ten adds iti shushruma dhiranam: thus we have heard from the wise. Shushruma comes from the same root as shruti, the Hindu name for the Vedas themselves: what is heard, passed from teacher to student. Now the debate. What do vidya and avidya mean here? Shankara reads avidya as ritual works and vidya as worship of the gods; each alone falls short. Sri Aurobindo hears vidya as knowing the One and avidya as knowing the many, and says a full life needs both. They disagree on the pair. They agree on the warning: learning that only puffs you up is its own kind of dark. The Mundaka Upanishad even calls study of the Vedas the lower knowing, and the knowing of the Imperishable the higher. And this is the tradition that sets its books before Saraswati to be blessed. It loves learning. It just asks what the learning is for.
screen: `DARKNESS, AND GREATER DARKNESS.` · `IVA: A PICTURE, NOT A VERDICT.` · `SHRUTI, AND SHANKARA'S READING.` · `AUROBINDO: THE ONE AND THE MANY.` · `WHAT IS THE LEARNING FOR?`

segments.voice: Vedanta names three steps of study: shravana, hearing; manana, thinking it over; nididhyasana, taking it to heart. Today, just the first. Listen the way a student once listened to the wise: no notes, no answers. Let one sound at a time come and go, near and far, without naming it. If you pray, say Om once, softly, and listen to it fade.
Reading the Isha in the original, verses nine and ten: iva, as it were, and iti shushruma, thus we have heard. A warning, not against learning, but against learning alone.
screen: `READING THE ISHA IN THE ORIGINAL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: vidya, learning that frees, not learning that puffs up. Shvetaketu found out at twenty-four. Until the next verse.

screen: `DAY 1494 COUNTS.` → `VIDYA: LEARNING THAT FREES, NOT LEARNING THAT PUFFS UP.` → `TOMORROW: CAN A KING TEACH A MONK?`

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: shruti, what is heard, the Hindu name for the Vedas, from the same root as shushruma.

what a scholar hears: iva softens the comparative bhuyah; Shankara takes vidya as devata-jnana and avidya as karma, Aurobindo as knowledge of unity and of multiplicity; the Mundaka's para and apara vidya make the same distinction another way.

chat.meaning: Iva, as it were, makes the verse a picture, not a verdict: darkness for delighting in knowing alone. Shvetaketu came home proud and missing the one teaching; the same tradition blesses its books before Saraswati.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 10 (anyad evahur vidyaya anyad ahur avidyaya; iti shushruma dhiranam ye nas tad vicacakshire)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–3 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four, conceited; Uddalaka asks about the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5 (two knowings: the lower, including the four Vedas; the higher, by which the Imperishable is grasped)
Shankara, commentary on Isha Upanishad 9–11 (avidya as karma, ritual works; vidya as knowledge and worship of deities)
Sri Aurobindo, Isha Upanishad commentary (vidya and avidya as knowledge of unity and of multiplicity)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (the self is to be heard, reflected on and meditated on: shrotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyah; the basis of shravana, manana, nididhyasana)
